modules.summary: What makes a four sided figure a quadrilateral, and the carpenter's puzzle that drives the chapter.

media.title: The Gate That Would Not Stay Square
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening on why four sides are not enough, and withholds everything that follows: no property is stated, no angle sum is given and no family is drawn. Students arrive with triangles from Class 7.
media.description: A carpenter builds a gate with four equal sides, yet by evening it sags into a lopsided shape until a triangular brace locks it firmly in place. The same thing happens on paper: four straight lines can make a neat closed figure, a tangled shape that crosses itself, or a figure that never closes at all. Some earn the name quadrilateral and some do not. A four-sided frame can slide through an entire family of shapes without changing the length of any side, while a triangle given the same treatment refuses to budge. So four sides alone do not determine a shape, and even a familiar name has to be earned by the properties the figure actually satisfies.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about what actually fixes the shape of a four sided figure. Key teaching points: 1) A four sided frame can change shape without changing any side. 2) A triangle cannot. 3) Equal sides do not force a square. 4) Names must be earned by properties, not by appearance. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often name a shape from how it looks on the page. 2) Students often think equal sides are enough to fix a figure. Pause points: 0:29, at the end of a brace stops it: ask why the gate sagged when every side stayed the same. 1:15, just before the opening question: ask what the brace actually added. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what makes a shape a square rather than a rhombus. After viewing, ask why builders use diagonal braces.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT

Show that four equal sides do not force a unique shape, then contrast this with the rigidity of a triangle and with four-line figures that may or may not qualify as quadrilaterals. Open the question of what properties actually make a quadrilateral and what forces a shape to stay fixed, without teaching the criteria or answer.

STORY

A carpenter builds a gate with four equal sides, but the frame sags into a lopsided shape. A triangular brace stops the movement immediately. On paper, four straight lines can produce a neat closed figure, a tangled figure that crosses itself, or a figure that never closes. A four-sided frame can also slide through a whole family of shapes while keeping every side the same length, whereas a triangle refuses to deform under the same treatment. Some four-line figures earn the name quadrilateral and some do not. The film ends by asking what smallest set of facts forces a quadrilateral to be the intended shape.

RENDERER

Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter

Background: dark slate #1F2937.
Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

ASSETS

No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL

Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.

THE GATE

The gate is built with four equal sides.
It sags into a lopsided shape by the evening.
No side changes length during the sagging.

THE TRIANGULAR BRACE

A triangular brace is added across the gate.
After the brace is added, the sagging stops.
A triangle given the same treatment refuses to deform.

THE FOUR-SIDED FRAME

A four-sided frame can be pushed gently.
It slides through a whole family of different shapes.
None of its four side lengths changes.

FOUR LINES ON PAPER

Four straight lines can produce:
a neat closed figure,
a tangled figure that crosses itself,
or a figure that never closes.

QUADRILATERAL QUESTION

Some four-line figures earn the name quadrilateral.
Some do not.

Named disqualifiers:
a single curved edge,
and one crossing.

SHAPE NAMES

Four equal sides do not automatically make a square.
Names such as rhombus, parallelogram and kite have to be earned by properties.

WITHHELD

The complete three rules for being a quadrilateral.
The complete family tree of quadrilaterals.
The angle sum.
The exact conditions that force a particular quadrilateral.
Any later theorem, formula or method.

ANIMATION RULES

Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
No decorative-only animation.

The four-sided frame must visibly deform while keeping every side length unchanged.
The triangular brace must visibly prevent the corresponding deformation.
The three four-line outcomes must be visually distinct.
A crossing figure must visibly cross itself.
An open figure must visibly fail to close.
Do not introduce the missing quadrilateral criteria during the animation.

MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, HIGHEST PRIORITY

100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8.
Correct notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8 textbook.
Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning.
If a figure is not to scale it must say so on screen.
No transformation may pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

LANGUAGE

British spelling.
No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on screen.
Readable aloud by a student of this grade.
Indian names and places for any person or setting.

NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS

No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
No revealing of the complete three rules.
No formula or theorem from a later part of the chapter.
No worked solution.
No general statement of the method.
No text outside the safe margin.
No overlapping labels.
No external assets, watermarks or branding.
No particles, sparkles or glow.

SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT

1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
9. The complete quadrilateral criteria are never revealed.
10. The triangle's rigidity and the four-sided frame's flexibility are shown visually.
11. The crossing and open figures are clearly distinguishable.
12. The final frame is an open question, not an answer.
13. The film closes on curiosity about what properties actually force a quadrilateral to be the intended shape.

media.context: This opens the quadrilaterals chapter with the three conditions a figure must meet: closed with no gap, four straight sides, and sides meeting only at their endpoints. media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a failing figure shown without its cross; a valid figure with a side count other than four; a failure panel that breaks more than one condition without saying so; a corner drawn as two separate points; a closed figure described as open
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A plain quadrilateral is drawn at the left with its four corners marked as single points and its four sides labelled, ticked in a teal circle. Three condition cards run beside it, each ticked: the outline is closed with no gap, all four sides are straight, and the sides meet only at their endpoints. To the right, three failure panels are drawn smaller and crossed: one with a gap in the outline, one with a curved side, and one where two sides cross partway along so a corner is not an endpoint, each labelled with the condition it breaks. A word tag at the foot reads that quadrilateral comes from quadri meaning four and latus meaning side. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: closed with no gap; four straight sides; sides meet only at their endpoints; a quadrilateral; a gap in the outline; a curved side; sides crossing partway along; quadri means four, latus means side.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The valid figure must be closed, with exactly four straight sides meeting only at endpoints.
All three condition cards must be ticked for the valid figure.
Each failure panel must break exactly one named condition and must be crossed.
The word origin must be given as quadri for four and latus for side.
Every corner of the valid figure must be a single marked point.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Quad Dragger
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch. 4 Quadrilaterals (formerly NCERT Ch. 3 Understanding Quadrilaterals), sections on the parallelogram and its special cases. This is the chapter opener and it runs BEFORE any family is named or any property is proved, so nothing here is justified by a criterion the class has not met: the families are held BY CONSTRUCTION and the tool only reports what the construction does and does not fix. The hierarchy is inclusive, as the chapter states it: the rectangle keeps all four of the parallelogram's statements and adds two, which the tool shows as the count 0 subset 4 subset 6.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the drag that breaks or fails to break the property.
whatYouLearned: A property forced by the construction survives every legal position
A property that one drag switches off was only true of the drawn case
Turning a figure never changes a verdict, because every verdict is read from the measures

overview.goal: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A light coordinate grid on a plain working ground, the way a shape is pinned out on squared paper with its corners still free to move. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class looks at one drawn parallelogram, calls it a rectangle because it looks like one, and the figure itself is asked to settle whether those right angles were ever really there.
overview.concept: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
overview.purpose: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. The property panel sits under the readouts. No two vertex handles are ever drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the property panel while a prediction is still open, and never render a self crossing or flattened figure. A degenerate figure would give the readouts nothing honest to say.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A property that holds in the drawn position is not the same as a property the construction forces. Breaks: A property judged from a single drawn case, so a parallelogram that happens to look like a rectangle is credited with right angles. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Verdicts come from the measures, so turning a figure never changes what it keeps. Breaks: Prototypical images, where a figure is recognised only in its standard orientation and not when it is turned. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Failing to break a property is evidence; the construction that forces it is the reason. Breaks: Treating a run of unbroken drags as a proof, so a property that merely survived is filed as forced. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A refused position protects the readouts; a degenerate figure has nothing honest to report. Breaks: Expecting the tool to draw any four points and grade them, so a degenerate case is read as a bug. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The kept list is a property of the construction, so a figure built with no constraints keeps nothing. Breaks: Reading the property panel as a description of the shape on screen rather than of how it was built.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the constructed parallelogram with the property panel hidden and the readouts on, and ask the class to say out loud which measurements will stay equal when a corner moves. Commit the class list on the prediction pad. Target family parallelogram, the opening four vertices. Never show the property panel before the prediction is committed, and never name a surviving property at this call. Call 2. Move one corner through three separate named positions and let the class watch which ticks hold and which go out. Point at the property panel and then at the kept list. Target family parallelogram, one vertex moved to three positions in turn. Read every side, angle and diagonal number you state from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Switch the family to free with the same list of statements still on screen and point at the statements that go out. Target family free. Say how many statements the kept list still holds, reading the count from the tool's own state and never from memory.

LOCK ONE SIDE: lock a side length, then find how much of the figure is still free to move.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The construction fixes opposite sides equal, so every legal position was built to satisfy it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The two opposite side readouts move together through every drag and their ticks never go out
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A property the construction forces cannot fail, which is why no drag breaks it

observationsAndConclusions.why: Nothing in the parallelogram construction ties the two diagonal lengths to each other, so they agree only where the figure happens to be a rectangle
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The equal diagonals tick lights in one position and goes out on the very next drag
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: True in the drawn case and guaranteed by the family are two different claims

observationsAndConclusions.why: A free figure is built with no relation fixed, so there is nothing holding any statement in place
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The same list of statements put against a free quadrilateral keeps almost nothing
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The kept list describes how a figure was built, not how it currently looks

media.description: A quadrilateral stands on squared paper with four draggable corners, its equal sides marked with matching hatch strokes, its equal angles with matching arcs and every right angle with the small square the textbook uses. Beside it eight statements each carry a live tick that lights only while the statement holds at the position on screen, and a badge that says whether the CONSTRUCTION keeps it. Dragging is what separates the two: the four statements a parallelogram is built to satisfy never go out however the figure is pulled about, while equal diagonals and four right angles light up in the one position where the parallelogram happens to look like a rectangle and are struck through the moment the next drag lands, labelled with the position number that broke them. The same eight statements are then put to a free quadrilateral, where not one of them survives, so the kept list reads as a fact about how a figure was built rather than about how it currently looks. Side lengths, angles, both diagonal lengths and the two halves at O are all derived from one measure function on the stored vertex coordinates, so no two numbers on the screen can disagree, and near collinear, self crossing, zero length and off paper positions are refused before the drag completes with the reason drawn at the corner that caused it.

scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The figure, every readout, the property panel, every control, no score and no question. A free quadrilateral on the grid with all readouts on and every vertex draggable.
scenes.animation: Drag update: sides, angles and diagonals recompute in the same frame as the handle moves, so no readout ever lags the figure.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Equal sides are marked with matching ticks and equal angles with matching arcs. A property that survives every drag is written in the kept list, one that does not is left out.
concept.statement: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
prerequisites: the names of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: A property judged from a single drawn case, so a parallelogram that happens to look like a rectangle is credited with right angles.
Prototypical images, where a figure is recognised only in its standard orientation and not when it is turned.
concept.why_it_is_true: The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure.
worked_numbers: In a constructed parallelogram the opposite sides stay equal through every drag, and the readouts move together.
In the same parallelogram the diagonals are equal only in the positions where it happens to be a rectangle, and one drag switches that tick off.
In a free quadrilateral even the opposite sides stop being equal, so almost nothing is kept.

extra: A folding clothes rack whose opposite arms stay equal however far it is opened
A criss cross expanding gate that keeps its bars parallel all the way along its track
A hinged pencil box lid that keeps the same width at every opening angle
A photograph of a tilted window frame that still measures as a rectangle
A rubber band stretched over four pegs and then lifted onto one new peg
A cardboard carton flattened and reopened, with its opposite faces still the same size
textbook: The rectangle set out as a list of conditions, so membership is decided by checking rather than by looking
Asking whether opposite sides being parallel and equal is enough on its own to make a quadrilateral a rectangle
Judging the claim that a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square
Reading the angles inside a rectangle from the equal halves its two diagonals cut

lockSideOutcomes.side0: the bottom side is fixed and only the opposite side and the two angles at its ends can still change
lockSideOutcomes.side1: the right hand side is fixed, and the readouts mark which measures are now determined
lockSideOutcomes.side2: the top side is fixed, and because the family already forces opposite sides equal the bottom side is fixed with it
lockSideOutcomes.side3: the left hand side is fixed, leaving the figure one free direction to slide in

setFamilyOutcomes.free: the four corners move independently, and every statement in the panel goes out somewhere, so the kept list empties
setFamilyOutcomes.rectangle: every parallelogram tick stays lit and equal diagonals and four right angles join them, so six statements survive instead of four
setFamilyOutcomes.parallelogram: opposite sides equal, opposite angles equal, next door angles adding to 180 and the diagonals bisecting each other all stay lit through every drag; equal diagonals and right angles flicker

showReadoutsOutcomes.on: the four side lengths, the four angles and both diagonal lengths are on screen and recompute with the figure
showReadoutsOutcomes.off: the measures are hidden and the ticks have to be judged from the marks alone

showPropertiesOutcomes.on: the candidate statements and their live ticks appear beside the figure
showPropertiesOutcomes.off: the panel is hidden, which is the only legal state while a prediction is still open

answer_key.worked: A property that survives every legal drag is guaranteed by the family; one that switches off under dragging was only true of the drawn case.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: which listed properties hold at the current vertices, and which of them are forced by the family rather than incidental.
answer_key.precision: All measures are derived from the stored vertex coordinates. Equality is judged with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, and the tolerance is stated in the feedback rather than hidden.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(vertices) = the four side lengths, four angles and two diagonal lengths, computed from the points. holds(property, measures) = the predicate evaluated at the current position. alwaysHolds(family, property) = the family's true property set, held as data and never inferred from the drawn case.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: Near collinear vertices
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with a minimum separation, and the reason is stated on screen. A flattened quadrilateral has undefined angles, so the tool refuses the position rather than rendering a degenerate figure.

edge_cases.case: A self crossing configuration
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked before the drag completes. Sides may meet only at their endpoints, so a crossing figure is not a quadrilateral and is refused rather than drawn and marked wrong.

edge_cases.case: A zero length side
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with the reason on screen. Three points and a repeat is a triangle, not a four sided figure.

edge_cases.case: A parallelogram dragged into a rectangle
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The extra ticks light and the tool says they are true here but not kept, because one further drag turns them off. This is the case the whole tool exists for.

edge_cases.case: A figure dragged into an unusual orientation
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Every property is evaluated from the measures, not from the picture, so a tilted rectangle keeps every tick a level one keeps. Orientation never changes a verdict.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'which_always', family:string, properties:string[]} | {kind:'break_it', family:string, property:string} | {kind:'name_family', keptList:string[]} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showReadouts.description: Show the four side lengths, four angles and both diagonal lengths beside the figure.

startingFamily.description: Which construction the figure opens in: free, parallelogram or rectangle.

constraints: A constructed parallelogram stays a parallelogram no matter how it is dragged. The family is enforced by construction, never by correcting the figure after the fact.
Collinear vertices, self crossing configurations and zero length sides are all blocked before the drag completes, each with its reason on screen.
Vertices are stored as points and every side, angle and diagonal is derived from them, so no two readouts can disagree.
Equality checks use a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, and the tolerance is stated in the feedback.
An answer that a property holds because it looks that way is rejected; the tool asks the student to name the part of the construction that forces it.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The figure on its grid, the measurement readouts, the property panel, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: a constructed parallelogram is drawn with the property panel HIDDEN. The class commits which measurements will stay equal, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Drag: a vertex moves through several positions and the readouts change while the forced ticks stay lit, with the committed guess held beside the kept list.
Free figure: the same statements are put against a free quadrilateral and most of them flicker off, so kept and merely true stand apart.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the kept list is on screen beside the free figure. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: A constructed parallelogram on a light grid with readouts on and the property panel hidden, the predict pad open on 'Drag any corner of this parallelogram. Which measurements do you think will stay equal?'.

normal.shows: The figure, every readout, the property panel, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A free quadrilateral on the grid with all readouts on and every vertex draggable.
play_modes: BREAK IT IF YOU CAN: pick one statement the parallelogram keeps and hunt for a position that switches it off.
TRUE HERE ONLY: find three positions of the parallelogram where an extra tick lights, and say what turns each off.
TILT TEST: drag a rectangle into three unusual orientations and check that not one tick changes.
LOCK ONE SIDE: lock a side length, then find how much of the figure is still free to move.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example moving a vertex to a position a child suggests to test whether a tick survives it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

media.title: Introduction to Quadrilaterals and the Rectangle Definition
media.context: Plays on M1.S1.T1.C6, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 150-second whiteboard-style explainer on a pure white canvas. It opens with three everyday four-sided shapes drawn flat in Navy Blue, a door, a window pane, and a chessboard surface, each with its four interior angles marked by small arcs. A row of five figures labelled (i) to (v) then appears; (i), (ii), (iii) stay filled pale yellow as four-sided closed figures while (iv) a curved-side shape and (v) a self-crossing shape each receive an Orange cross. A single quadrilateral ABCD is then drawn, its four vertices labelled and the angles ∠A, ∠B, ∠C, ∠D lighting up in Orange one at a time. Finally a chalkboard rectangle is checked against a two-item on-screen checklist: the four right-angle marks appear in Orange, the matching opposite sides flash with tick marks, and a Dark Green tick confirms "rectangle".
media.teaching_notes: Play this video at the very start of the chapter, before any worked classification, to introduce the word quadrilateral and the rectangle definition. Pause around 0:40, just after the five figures appear and before the Orange crosses are stamped, and let students decide for themselves which figures are quadrilaterals and why, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment, so ask "Which of these five are quadrilaterals, and what two things must be true for a four-sided figure to qualify?" before resuming. Pause again around 1:30, after the four right-angle marks appear on the chalkboard but before the opposite-side ticks, and ask "We have confirmed all four corners are right angles, what is the second condition you still need to check before you can call it a rectangle?" so students predict the second condition before it is revealed.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 150 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal. Background pure white. Font: Lilly. Scene sequence (5 scenes): Scene 1 (0-25s): Three everyday objects, a door, a window pane, and a chessboard surface, are sketched flat in Navy Blue, each with four interior angle arcs. Narrator: "Look around the room, the door, the window, a chessboard. Each is a closed four-sided figure, and mathematicians call these quadrilaterals, from the Latin quadri for four and latus for sides." Scene 2 (25-60s): A row of five figures labelled (i) to (v) is drawn. Figures (i), (ii), (iii) are four-sided closed figures filled pale yellow; (iv) has a curved side and (v) is self-crossing. Narrator pauses: "Before I reveal it, look at each shape and decide: what would you do next to tell a quadrilateral from the rest?" After the pause, an Orange cross is stamped on (iv) and (v). Narrator: "Notice how only the closed, straight-sided, four-sided figures qualify." Scene 3 (60-90s): A single quadrilateral ABCD is drawn in Navy Blue with vertices A, B, C, D labelled. Each interior angle ∠A, ∠B, ∠C, ∠D lights up in Orange in turn with a handwritten arc. Narrator: "The angles of a quadrilateral are simply the angles between its sides at each vertex, here, angle A, B, C, and D." Scene 4 (90-125s): A chalkboard rectangle appears beside a two-item checklist written in grey. Item (i) "all angles are right angles (90 degrees)", four right-angle marks appear in Orange at the corners, each drawn at exactly 90 degrees. Item (ii) "opposite sides are equal", top and bottom edges flash with equal tick marks, then the two vertical edges with equal tick marks. Narrator: "The key insight here is that a rectangle must satisfy two conditions together, every angle a right angle, and opposite sides equal in length." Scene 5 (125-150s): Both checklist items receive a Dark Green tick and the caption "rectangle" is written in Dark Green. Beside it a slanted four-sided figure with two clearly acute and two clearly obtuse corners is drawn in grey; an Orange cross marks its non-right corners and a grey cross stamps the figure. Narrator: "Both conditions hold, so the board is a rectangle. But fail even one, here the corners are not right angles, and it is not a rectangle. A definition is a checklist that draws the exact boundary of a class." Narration style: calm, instructional, using phrases like "Notice how..." and "The key insight here is...". Music: none, or very subtle. Visual elements: the 5-colour palette, Navy Blue for structure and invariant parts (the shape outlines and the fixed quadrilateral), Orange for the part being changed or highlighted (the angle arcs and right-angle marks being checked), pale yellow for soft highlight (qualifying figures), grey for secondary elements (the checklist text and the rejected shape), white canvas; arrows and tick marks showing the matching of opposite sides. Givens shown in Navy Blue, the checking operation in Orange, and the final confirmed answer in Dark Green. Every right angle drawn at exactly 90 degrees within 1 degree; opposite sides marked equal are drawn equal in length; the rejected slanted figure is drawn with genuinely non-right corners so the visuals match the narration exactly.

topics.summary: A quadrilateral is a closed figure with exactly four straight sides that meet only at their endpoints. The learner sorts figures into quadrilaterals and non quadrilaterals and names the parts of one that qualifies.

content.text: A quadrilateral is a closed figure made of exactly four straight sides, where the sides meet only at their endpoints. The word comes from the Latin quadri, meaning four, and latus, meaning side. Three things must all be true: the outline is closed with no gap, all four sides are straight segments, and neighbouring sides meet only at their corners so no side crosses another. A figure that has a curved side, an open gap, a crossing, or a different number of sides is not a quadrilateral. When a figure does qualify, it has four corners called vertices, four angles (one at each vertex, the angle between the two sides meeting there), and two diagonals joining opposite vertices.

media.title: Deduction 4, All Angles 90° Forces a Rectangle
media.context: Plays on M2.S2.T2.C12, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 165-second whiteboard-style walkthrough on a pure white canvas opens with quadrilateral ABCD, all four corners stamped with 90 degree squares in Navy Blue beside the caption "Do we need both parts?", as an Orange attempt to stretch one side longer flashes and snaps back. Diagonal BD is drawn in Orange, splitting the shape into triangle BAD and triangle DCB which shade in two soft greys, then matching marks light up one pair at a time: the 90 degree marks at A and C, the common side BD with a double tick, and the equal arcs of angle 1 at D and angle 2 at B. Captions read "Step 1", "Step 2", "Step 3" as the AAS match locks in and the equal opposite sides AD = CB and DC = BA reveal in Dark Green with tick marks. A closing card writes the simplified definition in Dark Green.
media.teaching_notes: Play this video after students have spent the suggested two minutes trying to construct a four-right-angled quadrilateral with unequal opposite sides and found it impossible - it then proves why their attempt had to fail. Pause around 0:25, right after the narrator asks the learner to picture building such a shape, and let the class predict whether it can be done before the diagonal is drawn (an attempt-before-reveal moment). Pause again around 1:10, just before angle 1 = angle 2 is established, and ask "why does angle 1 have to equal angle 2 here?" so students recall the angle 3 + angle 1 = 90 degrees reasoning from the earlier deduction rather than being told. As a follow-up, ask "which congruence condition fits two angles and a non-included side?" before the AAS label appears on screen.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 165 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal. Background pure white. Font: Lilly. Scene sequence (5 scenes): Scene 1 (0:00-0:25), states the idea. Quadrilateral ABCD appears with all four corners stamped 90 degrees in Navy Blue. Narrator: "The rectangle definition has two parts - four right angles and equal opposite sides. Do we really need both?" An Orange attempt tries to stretch one side longer while keeping the corners square; it snaps back. Narrator: "Try to picture a four-right-angled shape with unequal opposite sides - what would you do next to build one?" Pause here for the learner to attempt before the reveal. Scene 2 (0:25-0:55), sets up given and to-find. Captions list GIVEN angle A = angle B = angle C = angle D = 90 degrees in Navy Blue and TO PROVE AD = CB and DC = BA in grey. Diagonal BD is drawn in Orange. Narrator: "Notice how joining BD splits ABCD into two triangles, BAD and DCB. We will show they are congruent." Scene 3 (0:55-1:25), reveal step one at a time. The 90 degree marks at A and C light up; BD gains a double tick. Narrator: "Two equalities are already here - the right angles at A and C, and the shared side BD." Then angle 1 at D and angle 2 at B appear in Orange. Narrator: "The key insight here is to match one more pair of angles. Since angle B is 90 degrees, angle 3 plus angle 1 equals 90 degrees; in the lower triangle angle 3 plus angle 2 also equals 90 degrees. So angle 1 equals angle 2." Scene 4 (1:25-2:20), finish the deduction. The two equal angles and the non-included side BD highlight together. Narrator: "Two angles and a side that is not between them - that is the AAS condition, so triangle BAD is congruent to triangle DCB." The corresponding sides AD = CB and DC = BA reveal in Dark Green with tick marks. Narrator: "Therefore the opposite sides are equal - the angle condition alone gave us side-equality for free." content.text:
A rectangle can be defined in two different ways, and the chapter shows that the two say exactly the same thing.

The first definition uses the angles. A rectangle is a quadrilateral in which the angles are all 90 degrees.

The second definition uses the diagonals. A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other. This is the definition the Carpenter's Problem leads to.

Two definitions that pick out exactly the same figures are called equivalent, and either may be used as the starting point. A square is a rectangle whose four sides are also equal in length, so every square is a rectangle while not every rectangle is a square.

content.text: A rectangle is the quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other, meaning they cross at the midpoint of each. When these two conditions hold, the four endpoints always form a rectangle, and the angle at which the diagonals cross makes no difference to this. If the diagonals are unequal, the shape leans into a parallelogram instead, and if they do not cross at their midpoints, it is not a rectangle either. Turning this around, the diagonals of any rectangle are guaranteed to be equal and to bisect each other. This is exactly what the carpenter needs: two equal strips joined at their midpoints.

content.text: When the two equal diagonals of a rectangle cross, they cut the figure into four triangles. Because the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, all four half diagonals are equal, so each triangle is isosceles. If the diagonals cross at an angle x, then at a corner the diagonal splits the 90 degree corner into two parts: one part is (180 minus x) divided by 2, and the other is x divided by 2. These two parts always add to 90 degrees, which is why every corner of the figure is a right angle whatever the crossing angle. When x is 90, both parts become 45, the special square case.

content.text: A square is a rectangle in which the diagonals also cross at a right angle. It already inherits everything a rectangle has: equal diagonals that bisect each other and four right angle corners. The extra condition, that the diagonals meet at 90 degrees, forces all four sides to become equal, and that is what makes it a square. So the diagonals of a square are equal, bisect each other, and are perpendicular, and each diagonal cuts a corner into two 45 degree halves. Watch the boundaries: equal bisecting diagonals that are not perpendicular give only a rectangle, and perpendicular bisecting diagonals that are not equal give a rhombus, not a square. A handy fact is that a square's area equals its diagonal squared, divided by two.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state both definitions of a rectangle, one by all four angles being 90 degrees and one by the diagonals being equal and bisecting each other, and state that a square is a rectangle with all four sides equal. They will test a given quadrilateral against either definition and explain why the two definitions agree.

Students will be able to infer what two crossing strips must satisfy to trace a rectangle through observation and reasoning, and determine that four endpoints form a rectangle exactly when the diagonals are equal in length and cross at their shared midpoints, whatever angle they cross at. They will explain that unequal diagonals lean the figure into a parallelogram and off centre crossings fail, so a rectangle's own diagonals are always equal and bisect each other.

Students will be able to infer what the crossing angle of the equal diagonals fixes at each corner through observation and reasoning, and determine that a crossing angle x splits a right angle corner into a half of 180 minus x and a half of x, which always add to 90 degrees. They will explain that all four corner triangles are isosceles because the half diagonals are equal, and that when x is 90 both corner parts become 45, the special square case.

Students will be able to infer what one extra condition turns a rectangle into a square through observation and reasoning, and determine that equal diagonals which bisect each other and also cross at a right angle force all four sides equal. They will explain that the perpendicular crossing is the single extra demand beyond a rectangle, that a square's diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90 degrees, and that each diagonal cuts a corner into two 45 degree halves.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Understanding Quadrilaterals — the chapter's first general result, read after the student has been dragging figures and now needs something that holds for all of them at once. The class already tore the three corners of a TRIANGLE into a straight line in Class 7, and this tool is built on that memory: four corners make a whole turn, not a straight line. No similarity criterion, no polygon formula and no exterior-angle result is used, because none of them has been met yet; the diagonal and the triangle angle sum are the only facts the argument leans on.

overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A working sheet with the quadrilateral drawn on one side and a bare meeting point waiting on the other, the way torn paper corners are gathered around a single dot. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. overview.concept: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. Tearing the corners and fitting them round a point shows it for the figure in front of you. Cutting the figure with a diagonal into two triangles shows it for every quadrilateral at once, because every quadrilateral splits that way and every triangle has an angle sum of 180.
overview.purpose: The student shows the four angles fit together around a point, and chooses which of the two routes argues for every quadrilateral rather than for this one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure left and meeting point right on a wide frame, figure above and meeting point below on a 390 px frame. The total readout sits beside the meeting point at both widths. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never close the turn automatically. An automatic close would remove the only thing the student is meant to notice.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles whose angles together are exactly the four angles of the original, split between them. Two triangles give 180 plus 180, which is 360. Nothing in that argument depends on which quadrilateral was drawn, which is what makes it a proof rather than a demonstration. The tearing route is convincing but only about the figure that was torn. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The total is a test a set of angles either passes or fails, and a failing set describes no figure at all. Breaks: Believing any four angles can be drawn as a quadrilateral if the figure is squashed enough. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The result holds for concave figures too, because the two triangle argument never used convexity. Breaks: Believing the angle sum result only applies to figures that bulge outward everywhere. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): A demonstration on one figure and a proof about every figure are different acts, and only one survives reshaping. Breaks: A demonstration on one figure taken as a proof for all figures. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): An unfinished turn is a legal state whose gap measures exactly the missing angle. Breaks: Expecting the tool to complete the turn, so the missing corner is never measured. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The diagonal produces two triangles whose angles reassemble into the four original ones. Breaks: Angle sum recalled as 180 by carry over from triangles.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a quadrilateral, its corners untorn and the total HIDDEN, and asks whether the four angles will exactly fill a full turn, leave a gap or overlap. Beat 2 tears the corners and snaps them edge to edge at a point, closing the turn at 360. Beat 3 draws a diagonal instead, splitting the figure into two triangles for 180 plus 180, and then reshapes the original so the class can see which route survived the change. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with tearCorner, placeCorner, drawDiagonal and say.
whatYouLearned: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees
A diagonal splits any quadrilateral into two triangles, giving 180 plus 180
A demonstration on one figure is not a proof for every figure
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the quadrilateral with all four corners intact and the running total hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether the four corners will fill a full turn, leave a gap or overlap. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target the opening four angles. Never tear a corner before the prediction is committed, and never say the total at this call. Call 2. Tear the four corners and place them at the meeting point one at a time, pausing after each so the class can read the running total and the gap still to be filled. Target all four corners placed. Read the running total and the closing total from the tool's own readout, never from this plan. Call 3. Draw the diagonal, name the two triangles it makes, then reshape the original figure and show that the diagonal argument still holds while the torn demonstration would have to be started again. Target the diagonal on, then a reshaped quadrilateral. Say which of the two routes proves it for every quadrilateral, reading the tool's verdict from its own state.

hunts: GAP HUNT: tear three corners only and predict the gap before the readout shows it.
BEND IT IN: drag a corner inward and check the total again with the reflex angle counted.
IMPOSSIBLE SET: type four angles the tool refuses, then say by how much they miss.
RESHAPE AND RETEST: reshape the figure three times and watch which of the two routes has to be redone.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The four interior angles together sweep exactly one full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The four torn corners fit around the meeting point with no gap left and no overlap
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The angle sum of a quadrilateral is 360 degrees and not the 180 that triangles give

observationsAndConclusions.why: One diagonal always cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles, and two triangles always give 180 plus 180
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The reshaped figure still closes the turn even though every one of its angles changed
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The diagonal route argues for every quadrilateral, while the tearing route argues only for the figure that was torn

observationsAndConclusions.why: The total is fixed at 360, so any set that misses it cannot belong to a quadrilateral
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A stated set of angles that totals more than 360 leaves the turn overshot and is refused
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Refusing an impossible set is a conclusion about the set, not a failure of the tool

media.description: A lettered quadrilateral A B C D stands on a working sheet with a bare meeting point beside it, and each of its four interior angles is drawn as a coloured wedge of the SAME radius, so the area a corner covers is proportional to its measure. Tapping a corner tears the wedge off, leaving a dashed notch; dragging it to the meeting point snaps it edge to edge against whatever is already there, and a running total climbs while the turn still to be filled is drawn in a second accent until it closes. Concept beat 1 places only TWO wedges, so the Class 7 carry-over answer of 180 degrees arrives on screen as a straight angle with a glaring half-turn gap; beat 2 lands the other two and the readout reaches 360; beat 3 draws the diagonal that actually lies inside the figure, labels both triangles 180 degrees, and shows a DIFFERENT quadrilateral with its corners back on it, so the tearing would have to be redone while the diagonal argument is untouched. A vertex can be dragged in Free Play and the four angles are re-read off the drawn points; a drop that would fold the figure over itself is refused and the corner stays where it was. An angle set that does not total exactly 360, or carries a non positive angle, is refused BEFORE any figure is drawn, and refused with a number: the wedges are laid out anyway and the last one visibly rides over the first, with the overlap measured.

scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The figure, the meeting point, the total readout, every control, no score and no question. A reshapeable quadrilateral with all corners intact and every control live.
scenes.animation: Tear: the wedge lifts off the figure over 200 ms leaving a visible notch, so the angle is seen to move rather than to be copied.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Angles are marked with arcs at the vertices and keep their measures when torn. A full turn is 360 degrees and is drawn as the complete circle the four corners close.
concept.statement: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees. Tearing the corners and fitting them round a point shows it for the figure in front of you. Cutting the figure with a diagonal into two triangles shows it for every quadrilateral at once, because every quadrilateral splits that way and every triangle has an angle sum of 180.
prerequisites: the angle sum of a triangle is 180 degrees
misconceptions: Angle sum recalled as 180 by carry over from triangles.
A demonstration on one figure taken as a proof for all figures.
concept.why_it_is_true: A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles whose angles together are exactly the four angles of the original, split between them. Two triangles give 180 plus 180, which is 360. Nothing in that argument depends on which quadrilateral was drawn, which is what makes it a proof rather than a demonstration. The tearing route is convincing but only about the figure that was torn.
worked_numbers: Angles 100, 80, 100 and 80 add to 360 and the torn corners close exactly.
Three angles of 90, 85 and 100 leave a fourth of 85, because the total is fixed.
A set of 90, 90, 90 and 100 sums to 370, so no quadrilateral has those angles.

tearCornerOutcomes.cornerA: the first corner lifts away as a coloured wedge carrying its own measure, and the figure keeps its arc at that vertex
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerB: the second wedge lifts, and the running total on the meeting point climbs by that angle when it is placed
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerC: the third wedge lifts, and the gap readout shows how much of the turn is still open
tearCornerOutcomes.cornerD: the last wedge lifts, and placing it closes the turn exactly and the gap readout falls to zero

chooseRouteOutcomes.tearing: the tool accepts it as a demonstration for this figure and says plainly that it has to be repeated for any other figure
chooseRouteOutcomes.twoTriangles: the tool accepts it as a proof for every quadrilateral, because the argument never used which quadrilateral was drawn

drawDiagonalOutcomes.on: one diagonal is drawn and the figure separates visibly into two triangles, each with its own angle sum shown
drawDiagonalOutcomes.off: the diagonal is removed and the quadrilateral is whole again with its four arcs intact

answer_key.worked: The four angles add to 360 degrees, because a diagonal splits any quadrilateral into two triangles of 180 each.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: the missing fourth angle, or whether a stated set of four angles can belong to a quadrilateral at all.
answer_key.precision: Torn corners are rotated with exact transform matrices so the measured angles do not drift during a drag. Angle sets are validated as exact sums.
answer_key.ground_truth: angleSum(vertices) = the four interior angles, computed from the points, which always total 360. missingAngle(three) = 360 minus their sum. isValidSet(four) = every angle strictly positive and the total exactly 360.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A stated set that does not sum to 360
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected before any figure is drawn, with the shortfall or excess stated. The tool never renders a quadrilateral whose angles could not exist.

edge_cases.case: A non positive angle in a stated set
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Rejected with the reason on screen. A zero or negative angle is not a corner, so there is nothing to tear.

edge_cases.case: A concave quadrilateral
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Still sums to 360 and the tool allows it, with the reflex corner drawn as a reflex arc. Excluding it would suggest the result needs convexity.

edge_cases.case: A corner dragged away and back
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The torn corner keeps its exact measure throughout, so replacing it restores the figure exactly. No measure is recomputed from the dragged position.

edge_cases.case: Three corners placed and one missing
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The gap is shown and measured rather than the turn being closed automatically. An unfinished turn is a legal state and the size of the gap is informative.

hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'missing_angle', given:number[]} | {kind:'is_valid_set', angles:number[]} | {kind:'which_route'} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showDiagonal.description: Draw the diagonal that splits the figure into two triangles. Off until the second route.

startingAngles.description: The four interior angles the figure opens with, which must total exactly 360.

constraints: Torn corners keep their exact measures during the drag, rotated with exact transform matrices so no angle drifts by a fraction of a degree.
Angle sets that do not total exactly 360, or that contain a non positive angle, are rejected before a figure is drawn.
The turn is never closed automatically. A gap left by a missing corner is drawn and measured, because the gap is the evidence.
The two routes are held as separate arguments with separate state, so the student can compare them rather than seeing them merge.
The original figure can be reshaped at any time and the tool recomputes both routes, so a claim about all quadrilaterals is testable on the spot.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The quadrilateral, the meeting point, the torn corners, the total readout, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the quadrilateral is drawn with its corners untorn and the total HIDDEN. The class commits fill exactly, leave a gap or overlap, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Tear: the four corners come off and snap edge to edge at a common point, closing a full turn, and the readout lands on 360.
Two triangles: a diagonal splits the original into two triangles for 180 plus 180, and the figure is then reshaped to show which route survived.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the reshaped figure still gives 360 by the triangle route. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: A quadrilateral with all four corners intact, an empty meeting point and no total shown, the predict pad open on 'Do you think the four angles will exactly fill a full turn, leave a gap or overlap?'.

normal.shows: The figure, the meeting point, the total readout, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A reshapeable quadrilateral with all corners intact and every control live.
play_modes: GAP HUNT: tear three corners only and predict the gap before the readout shows it.
BEND IT IN: drag a corner inward and check the total again with the reflex angle counted.
IMPOSSIBLE SET: type four angles the tool refuses, then say by how much they miss.
RESHAPE AND RETEST: reshape the figure three times and watch which of the two routes has to be redone.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example reshaping the figure to a shape a child suggests and letting the triangle route hold.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

media.title: The Angles That Always Add Up
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the angle sum. Students know the triangle angle sum from Class 7. The film must not give the total and must not draw the diagonal.
media.description: Bend a four sided figure any way you like, push its corners in and out, and something stays fixed: its four angles always sum to the same total. Triangles famously add to one hundred and eighty degrees, so what do quadrilaterals add to?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find the angle sum of a quadrilateral and justify it by splitting the figure into triangles. Key teaching points: 1) The angle sum does not change when the figure is deformed. 2) One diagonal splits a quadrilateral into two triangles. 3) Each triangle contributes a hundred and eighty degrees. 4) So the four angles total three hundred and sixty degrees. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often expect the total to depend on the shape. 2) Students often draw both diagonals and count the angles twice. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of what is the number?: ask the class to guess the total before it is shown. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what one line inside the figure could reveal. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what a triangle's angles add to. After viewing, ask how many triangles a quadrilateral splits into.

topics.summary: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, because a diagonal splits it into two 180 degree triangles. The learner finds missing angles and sees why three right angles force the fourth.

content.text: The four angles of any quadrilateral always add up to 360 degrees. This never changes, however you reshape the figure by dragging its corners. The reason is that a single diagonal cuts the quadrilateral into two triangles. Each triangle has angles adding to 180 degrees, so the two triangles together give 180 plus 180 equals 360 degrees, and those angles are exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral. To find a missing angle, add the three angles you know and subtract from 360. This also explains why a quadrilateral can never have three right angles beside a fourth that is not right: three right angles use up 270 degrees, so the fourth is forced to be the remaining 90.

This never changes, however you reshape the figure by dragging its corners. The reason is that a single diagonal cuts the quadrilateral into two triangles. Each triangle has angles adding to 180 degrees, so the two triangles together give 180 plus 180 equals 360 degrees, and those angles are exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral. To find a missing angle, add the three angles you know and subtract from 360. This also explains why a quadrilateral can never have three right angles beside a fourth that is not right: three right angles use up 270 degrees, so the fourth is forced to be the remaining 90.

overview.goal: The student states which sides and angles are equal or supplementary in each named family, and writes the minimum set of properties that pins a family down.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A single quadrilateral on a plain ground with a family selector above it and a property checklist standing beside it, the way one figure is marked up in a notebook margin. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says that next door angles in a parallelogram must be equal because the opposite ones are, and a slow sweep of the whole shape is asked to settle which pair is which.
overview.concept: Each family fixes a particular pattern of equal and supplementary relations. In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. Adding one more condition moves you to a rectangle or a rhombus, and adding both gives a square, so the families differ by which relations they force and not by how they happen to look.
overview.purpose: The student states which sides and angles are equal or supplementary in each named family, and writes the minimum set of properties that pins a family down.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.

The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not fill a checklist row before its prediction is committed, and never mark a relation the family does not force. A mark the family cannot guarantee is a false property claim.

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. In a parallelogram a pair of adjacent angles sits between the same two parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180. The opposite angles are then each 180 minus the same value, so they are equal to each other. The colour coding and the linking arcs make those two different relations visually different, which is exactly where the confusion lives. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A relation that holds at one point of the sweep is a position, not a property of the family. Breaks: A property judged from the drawn case, so a parallelogram in a rectangle position is credited with right angles. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Reaching a special position does not add a property to the family that was swept. Breaks: Reading a coincidence at one parameter value as a new guaranteed property. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Equal and supplementary are different relations that coincide only at 90 degrees. Breaks: Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A mark is a claim the family forces, so an unmarked pair is a pair nothing guarantees. Breaks: Expecting every quadrilateral to carry the parallelogram marks, so a trapezium is read as one. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A proposed property set is refuted by one figure that satisfies it and sits outside the family. Breaks: Believing a set of properties that every member has is automatically enough to define the family.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.
