conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the parallelogram with the equal sides coloured, no arcs drawn and the checklist hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether next door angles add to 180 or are equal. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target family parallelogram at the opening parameter. Never draw an arc or reveal a checklist row before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Sweep the shape parameter slowly from one end of its range to the other and point at the linking arc as it holds while the angles themselves keep changing. Target family parallelogram, a sweep across the full parameter range. Read the two angle values and the linking arc total from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Change the family preset to rectangle with the same arcs still drawn, and ask the class what the extra condition bought. Target family rectangle. Say what the equal pair and the supplementary pair each now read, taking both numbers from the tool's own state.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each of them is 180 minus the same adjacent angle, so the two can never come apart
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Through the whole sweep the two opposite angle readouts stay equal to each other
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Opposite angles equal is forced by the parallelogram and not by the position it happens to be in

observationsAndConclusions.why: That pair lies between the same two parallel sides, so the two angles must together make a straight angle
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The linking arc on a next door pair reads 180 at every value of the sweep
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Adjacent angles are supplementary and not equal, which is exactly the pair students swap

observationsAndConclusions.why: Ninety and ninety are equal to each other and also add to 180, so the two relations agree at that one value
observationsAndConclusions.observe: At the rectangle preset the equal pair and the supplementary pair give the same number
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Agreement in one family is not sameness, which is why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from

media.description: One lettered quadrilateral stands on a plain ground with a property checklist beside it. Equal sides carry matching hatch ticks and a shared colour, equal angles carry same-radius arcs, the parallel pairs carry arrowhead chevrons, and every angle pair the family forces to add to 180 is joined by a linking arc that prints the SUM rather than the word supplementary. A shape parameter sweeps the figure inside its family, and the marks the family forces never flicker while a relation that merely happens to hold at one value is drawn dashed and captioned 'at this value only' — so a coincidence can be watched switching off. Switching the family preset from parallelogram to rectangle, rhombus or square ADDS one condition at a time and the checklist grows without ever resetting, which is how the inclusive classification is read off the list rather than off the outline. Free Play lets the student predict each checklist row before opening it and then test a proposed minimum property set, which the tool answers by drawing a figure that satisfies the set and sits outside the family. Practice serves a session drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, each item rendering the figure its own question describes, with the asked measure masked until the answer is in.

mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a parallelogram with the checklist HIDDEN and asks whether next door angles will add to 180 or be equal. Beat 2 sweeps the shape parameter while the equal sides hold their matching colours and the linking arcs on adjacent angles stay at 180. Beat 3 switches preset to a rectangle, where the same arcs now also read 90 each, so what the family adds is visible as a change in the marks. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFamily, sweep, revealRow and say. No drag: the agent sets the parameter by value, never by sweeping continuously.

concept.notation: Equal sides are drawn in matching colours, equal angles carry matching arcs, and a supplementary pair is joined by a single linking arc labelled 180.
concept.statement: Each family fixes a particular pattern of equal and supplementary relations. In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary. Adding one more condition moves you to a rectangle or a rhombus, and adding both gives a square, so the families differ by which relations they force and not by how they happen to look.
prerequisites: the angle sum of a quadrilateral
misconceptions: Opposite angles confused with adjacent ones, so the pair that is equal and the pair that is supplementary are swapped.
Equality assumed where supplementarity holds, so adjacent angles in a parallelogram are expected to be equal.
concept.why_it_is_true: In a parallelogram a pair of adjacent angles sits between the same two parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180. The opposite angles are then each 180 minus the same value, so they are equal to each other. The colour coding and the linking arcs make those two different relations visually different, which is exactly where the confusion lives.
worked_numbers: In a parallelogram with one angle of 70, the adjacent angle is 110 and the opposite angle is 70 again.
In a rectangle every one of those values is 90, so equal and supplementary agree by coincidence.
In a rhombus of side 6 all four sides share one colour, while the angles still split into two equal pairs.

extra: A sliding gate whose slanted bars keep their next door angles adding to a straight angle
A folding ironing board whose opposite legs keep the same angle as it opens
A window blind whose slats stay parallel at every setting
A bicycle stand leaning over, with its opposite bars still equal
A hand held paper fan whose ribs keep two matching angles
A book held open at a slant, so the page corners are no longer square
A diamond shaped road sign with four equal sides and not one right angle
A carrom board and a chess board, both with four equal sides and four right angles
A wall tile pattern where every slanted tile shares the same pair of angles
textbook: Constructing a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides that do not meet at right angles
Finding the remaining angles of a parallelogram when one of them is given
Finding the remaining angles of a trapezium from the angle already marked
Asking whether squares are the only quadrilaterals with all four sides equal
Finding all the sides and angles of the figure made by joining two equilateral triangles
Deciding what kind of quadrilateral has its opposite sides equal, using a diagonal and congruent triangles

answer_key.worked: In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles add to 180, and the same two relations survive the whole sweep.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: the missing side or angle in the named family, or which pairs the marks currently join.
answer_key.precision: Presets are defined by construction rules rather than fixed coordinates, so every measure is derived and the family cannot be left by sweeping. Equality uses a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(family, parameter) = the sides, angles and diagonals produced by the construction. equalPairs(measures) and supplementaryPairs(measures) = the pairs the marks join, evaluated live. minimalSet(family) = the smallest condition set whose figures are exactly that family.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

steps: The parallelogram construction forces 3 relations: the opposite sides are equal; the opposite angles are equal; next door angles add to 180.
Equal angles all round is not one of them.
This is one value of the sweep, where the figure sits in a rectangle position.

Sweeping on moves them apart again while the side colours stay put.

steps: Next door angles in any parallelogram add to 180.
In a rectangle each of them measures 90.
180 minus 90 is 90, so the supplement of one is the other.
The two relations agree here because 90 is its own supplement.

items.answer: No: they agree only because 90 is its own supplement, and they part company as soon as the angle moves

steps: A linking arc marks a pair the family forces to add to 180.
Only the two legs run between the single pair of parallel sides.
So only the angle pairs on those legs are co-interior.
The remaining pairs are not forced by anything, so marking them would claim a property the family does not give.
The trapezium therefore forces 0 of the listed relations.

steps: The proposed set is a claim that nothing outside the family can satisfy it.
The tool builds a figure that satisfies the set.
That figure has one pair of equal sides and no parallel pair at all.
It is outside the family, so the proposed set is too weak.
A set is minimum only when nothing outside the family can meet it.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the two relations side by side on one figure, because the misconception is that there is only one. The linking arc prints 70° + 110° = 180° while the two opposite arcs both read 70°: the class can see that the pair that is EQUAL and the pair that ADDS TO 180 are different pairs, and that they are marked with different devices for exactly that reason.

Beat 2 is the justification, and it needs motion. The figure is swept from one end of its range to the other; every number on screen changes and the same two marks hold throughout, because a pair of next-door angles sits between the same two parallel sides and is therefore co-interior. What survives the sweep is what the family guarantees — that is the whole argument and it cannot be made from a still frame.

Beat 3 adds one condition. The preset moves to a rectangle and the checklist GROWS: the three parallelogram rows stay ticked and a fourth lights. That is the inclusive hierarchy read off the list, and it is also where equal and supplementary agree — each next-door angle reads 90 and 90 is its own supplement — which is precisely why a rectangle is the worst figure to learn the difference from.

media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Use the parallel sides of a parallelogram to determine its angles, sides and diagonals. Key teaching points: 1) Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. 2) Neighbouring angles add to a straight angle. 3) Opposite sides are equal in length. 4) The diagonals cut each other exactly in half. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume all four angles of a parallelogram are equal. 2) Students often think the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of a hidden pattern: ask what the angle opposite a given one must be. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what happens where the diagonals cross. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask why the parallel sides lock the angles. After viewing, ask whether the diagonals are equal.

content.text: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. In any parallelogram, the opposite angles are equal, and each pair of adjacent angles (two angles sharing a side) adds up to 180 degrees. The reason is that a side acts as a transversal crossing the two parallel sides, and the two angles on the same side of it are co-interior angles, which are always supplementary. From this, if you know one angle you know them all: the opposite angle repeats it, and each neighbouring angle is its supplement. So the four angles read as a value, its supplement, the value again, and the supplement again, going around. When every angle is 90 degrees the parallelogram is a rectangle.

content.text: In a parallelogram the opposite sides are equal, so its perimeter is twice the sum of two adjacent sides. Its two diagonals always bisect each other, meaning they cross at a point that is the midpoint of both. However, the two diagonals do not have to be equal in length. As a parallelogram leans away from a rectangle, the diagonals keep their shared midpoint but stretch by different amounts, so they become unequal. Equal diagonals appear only in the special case where all the angles are 90 degrees, which is a rectangle. So bisecting is guaranteed for every parallelogram, but equal length is not.

As a parallelogram leans away from a rectangle, the diagonals keep their shared midpoint but stretch by different amounts, so they become unequal. Equal diagonals appear only in the special case where all the angles are 90 degrees, which is a rectangle. So bisecting is guaranteed for every parallelogram, but equal length is not.

topics.publication_chunk: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral whose opposite sides are parallel. In any parallelogram, the opposite angles are equal, and each pair of adjacent angles (two angles sharing a side) adds up to 180 degrees. The reason is that a side acts as a transversal crossing the two parallel sides, and the two angles on the same side of it are co-interior angles, which are always supplementary. So the four angles read as a value, its supplement, the value again, and the supplement again, going around. When every angle is 90 degrees the parallelogram is a rectangle. content.text: A rhombus is a quadrilateral in which all four sides are equal. Because its opposite sides turn out to be parallel, every rhombus is also a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are equal and its adjacent angles add to 180 degrees. This means the four angles follow from any one of them, exactly as in a parallelogram: a value, its supplement, and each repeated once. Its perimeter is four times one side. Equal sides do not by themselves make a square, though. A rhombus can lean, keeping all four sides equal while its angles are not 90 degrees. Only when the angles are also 90 degrees does the rhombus become a square.

content.text: The two diagonals of a rhombus always cross at right angles, bisect each other, and bisect the vertex angles they reach. Because they are perpendicular and bisect each other, they cut the rhombus into four right triangles whose legs are the two half diagonals. So each side of the rhombus is the hypotenuse of one of these right triangles, found from the half diagonals, and the area of the rhombus is half the product of its two diagonals. The perpendicular crossing is true for every rhombus, whether upright or leaning. It becomes a square only when the angles are also 90 degrees, and only then do the two diagonals become equal in length.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how the angles of a four equal sided figure behave through observation and reasoning, and determine that a rhombus is a parallelogram, so its opposite angles are equal and its adjacent angles add to 180 degrees, letting all four angles follow from any one. They will explain that equal sides alone do not make a square, since a leaning rhombus keeps its four equal sides while its angles move away from 90 degrees.

They will explain that this perpendicular crossing holds for every rhombus, so it is a square only when its angles are also 90 degrees and its diagonals become equal.

overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Diagonals fill the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and beneath on a 390 px frame. Every endpoint keeps a 44 px hit target and no two are drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the outline while a prediction is still open, and never report a single family name where the conditions allow more than one. A single name would teach that equal diagonals force a square.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the diagonal conditions from its own values, shows the question, then reveals the readouts, the outline and the family set together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A condition set names a family, and the family named here contains the square rather than being it. Breaks: Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A failed family test is reported as a named missing condition, not as no answer. Breaks: Diagonals treated as decoration, so a figure whose diagonals fail a condition is thought to have no family at all. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Diagonal conditions guarantee a whole chain of families, so the honest answer is a set. Breaks: Believing each condition set picks out exactly one shape name. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The crossing point is defined by both diagonals, so it cannot be moved off either of them. Breaks: Treating the crossing point as a free handle rather than as the meeting the conditions are measured from. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The outline exists only because the four endpoints are not all on one line. Breaks: Forgetting that the outline is built from the diagonals, so a degenerate crossing is expected to draw something.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with two diagonals that are equal and bisect each other, the outline HIDDEN, and asks what shape this must be. Beat 2 reveals the outline as a rectangle and the three readouts are read back as the reason. Beat 3 adds the right angle lock, the outline becomes a square, and the tool says that the earlier answer was a set and not a single shape. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setDiagonals, toggleRightAngle, revealOutline and say. No drag: the agent sets endpoints by position, never by sweeping.
whatYouLearned: Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram
Equal diagonals add the rectangle condition and a right angled crossing adds the rhombus condition
A condition set can name a set of families, because a square is a rectangle and a rhombus at once
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on two equal diagonals bisecting each other with the outline hidden and all three condition readouts on, and ask the class to name the family out loud. Commit the class name on the prediction pad. Target the two equal diagonals with the crossing at both midpoints. Never reveal the outline before the prediction is committed, and never name the family at this call. Call 2. Reveal the outline and read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. Target the outline on. Read both diagonal lengths and the crossing angle from the tool's own readouts, never from this plan. Call 3. Switch the right angle lock on with the same two diagonals in place, and let the outline change. Target the right angle lock on. Say which families the tool now lists in the family set readout, taking the list from the tool's own state and never from memory.

hunts: BUILD THE FAMILY: set the diagonals so the outline is a rhombus that is not a square, then say which condition you left out.
ONE CONDITION AT A TIME: start from a general crossing and turn on one condition at a time, naming what each buys.
NOT A SQUARE: make equal bisecting diagonals give three different rectangles, none of them square.
MISSING PIECE: aim at a target family, get it wrong on purpose, and read which condition the tool names.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The four diagonal endpoints joined in order are the whole figure, so the diagonals determine the outline completely
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The outline is drawn only after the three condition readouts have been read, and it is exactly what they promised
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The diagonals are a defining condition, not a feature to be read off the shape afterwards

observationsAndConclusions.why: Equal lengths and bisection together force the rectangle conditions and nothing further
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Equal diagonals that bisect each other give many different rectangles and only a few of them are squares
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Equal diagonals never force a square, because every rectangle that is not a square has them too

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, so the conditions compose instead of replacing each other
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Switching the right angle lock on turns the same crossing into a square
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A condition set can name more than one family, which is why the honest answer is sometimes a set of names

media.description: Two crossing segments stand alone on a plain working ground with no figure drawn around them: the diagonals AC and BD, meeting at O. Tick marks carry the bisection (one tick on each half of AC, two on each half of BD, drawn only where that diagonal really is cut in half), a small square at O carries the right-angled crossing, and both lengths and the crossing angle are printed live along the top of the scene. Three labelled booleans - bisect each other, equal in length, meet at right angles - sit beside the figure, and beneath it the tool prints the whole SET of families the current conditions guarantee rather than a single name, so a square is reported as sitting inside the rectangle set and the rhombus set at once. The outline is never drawn independently: it is the quadrilateral A B C D formed by joining the four endpoints in order, and it appears as a consequence of the conditions rather than as a separate piece of evidence. In Free Play the student drags any endpoint, slides the crossing along a diagonal, locks the crossing at 90 degrees and sets a target family, and the tool answers a failed target by NAMING the condition that is still missing. Two positions are refused with the reason on screen - a crossing that is not on both diagonals, and two diagonals dragged towards one straight line - because neither describes a figure that exists.

Beat 2 reveals the outline as a rectangle and the three readouts are read back as the reason. Beat 3 adds the right angle lock, the outline becomes a square, and the tool says that the earlier answer was a set and not a single shape. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setDiagonals, toggleRightAngle, revealOutline and say. No drag: the agent sets endpoints by position, never by sweeping.

concept.notation: The three diagonal conditions are written as bisect each other, equal in length and meet at right angles. A family answer may be a set of names, not a single name.
concept.statement: The diagonals decide the family. Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. Add equal lengths and it is a rectangle; add a right angle crossing instead and it is a rhombus; add both and it is a square. Because a square is a rectangle, a condition set can name more than one family at once, so the answer is a set.
prerequisites: the diagonal properties of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: Diagonals treated as decoration rather than as a defining condition, so they are read off a shape and never used to make one.
Equal diagonals assumed to force a square, ignoring every non square rectangle.
concept.why_it_is_true: The outline is always the quadrilateral formed by joining the four diagonal endpoints in order, so the diagonals fully determine it. Bisecting makes the two halves of each diagonal equal, which forces the opposite sides to match. Equal lengths then force equal diagonals in the outline, and a right angled crossing forces equal sides. Each condition adds exactly one constraint to the outline, which is why they compose.
worked_numbers: Diagonals of 10 and 10 bisecting each other give a rectangle, and only some of those are squares.
Diagonals of 10 and 6 bisecting at right angles give a rhombus that is not a square.
Diagonals of 8 and 8 bisecting at right angles give a square, which is in both of the earlier sets.

revealOutlineOutcomes.on: the four endpoints are joined in order by a thin stroke, and the family set readout is filled in
revealOutlineOutcomes.off: only the two crossing segments and the three condition readouts are on screen, which is the state a prediction is made in

setTargetFamilyOutcomes.kite: the target is met when one diagonal is bisected by the other and they meet at right angles, which the tool marks as the only target the bisect both condition must be dropped for
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.none: no target is set and the tool simply reports the family set the current conditions allow
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.square: the target needs all three conditions at once, and the tool reports the square as sitting inside both earlier sets
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.rhombus: the target is met when the diagonals bisect each other and the crossing angle readout reaches 90
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.rectangle: the target is met when the diagonals bisect each other and their two length readouts agree
setTargetFamilyOutcomes.parallelogram: the target is met as soon as the crossing point is the midpoint of both diagonals, whatever their lengths

toggleRightAngleOutcomes.on: the crossing is locked at 90 degrees and the crossing angle readout freezes there, so the outline gains four equal sides
toggleRightAngleOutcomes.off: the crossing angle is free again and the outline loses its equal sides unless the endpoints happen to keep them

answer_key.worked: Diagonals that are equal and bisect each other name the rectangle family, which includes the square, so the answer is a set and not one shape.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn diagonals: the three boolean conditions, the family set they imply, and whether a target family has been produced.
answer_key.precision: Every condition is measured from the endpoint coordinates with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, stated in the feedback. The ground truth is a set of family names, never a single name.
answer_key.ground_truth: bisect(d1, d2) = the crossing point is the midpoint of both. equal(d1, d2) = the two lengths agree within tolerance. perpendicular(d1, d2) = the crossing angle is 90 within tolerance. familySet(conditions) = every family name consistent with them, so a square condition set returns square inside rectangle and rhombus.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class commits a name with the outline NOT yet drawn. The three booleans are the only evidence on screen, which is the whole point: the diagonals have to become a defining condition rather than a feature read off a finished shape. Ask for the name out loud before moving on, and do not say the word square.

Beat 2 is the payoff and it is a consequence, not a new fact. The four endpoints join in order and a rectangle appears, so read the three conditions back one at a time as the reason it had to come out that way. The same 16 and 16 that were on screen a moment ago are still on screen.

Beat 3 adds ONE condition and the earlier answer is seen to have been a set all along. The crossing locks at 90 degrees, the outline becomes a square, and rectangle stays lit beside it. If rectangle went dark the tool would be teaching that a square is not a rectangle, which is the misconception the beat exists to break.

media.title: Name the Shape Before You Draw It
media.context: This hook opens the topic on naming a quadrilateral from its diagonals or from joined triangles. Students know the main families. The film must not match any clue to any shape and must not reveal the triangle surprise.
media.description: Imagine being handed only two crossing lines, told nothing about the corners, and asked to name the quadrilateral they will make. Three simple clues about those diagonals can name the shape before a single side is drawn.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Name a quadrilateral from properties of its diagonals, or from two joined triangles. Key teaching points: 1) Diagonals that bisect each other give a parallelogram. 2) Adding equal diagonals gives a rectangle. 3) Adding perpendicular diagonals instead gives a rhombus. 4) Both conditions together give a square. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think the diagonals cannot determine the shape. 2) Students often forget that two identical triangles can be joined in more than one way. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of three simple clues: ask which shape equal diagonals alone would give. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what two identical triangles could make. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the diagonals of a square do. After viewing, ask how many clues are needed to name a shape.

media.title: Parallelograms, Definition and the Shape Hierarchy
media.context: Plays on M5.S6.T6.C59, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 165-second whiteboard-style explainer on a pure white canvas. It opens on a Navy Blue rectangle whose right-angle marks fade out as the top and bottom edges slide sideways, slanting the shape into quadrilateral ABCD with both pairs of opposite sides carrying single and double Orange arrowheads and the caption 'parallelogram' appearing. A three-layer nested Venn diagram then draws itself, an outer 'Parallelogram' ellipse outlined in Orange, a 'Rectangle' ellipse outlined in Navy Blue inside it, and a 'Square' ellipse in pale yellow innermost, each layer labelled in handwritten text. The closing scenes show a ruler-and-set-square construction: segment AB = 4 cm and AD = 5 cm drawn at a 30° included angle in Navy Blue, then a line parallel to AB through D and a line parallel to AD through B meet in Orange at point C, with tick marks and on-screen captions reading 'Step 1' and 'Step 2'.
media.teaching_notes: Play this video when introducing the parallelogram as a concept, after students already know rectangle properties but before they attempt the remaining-angles question for themselves. First pause around 1:20, just after the narrator asks "what would you do next to reach a square?" and before the innermost ellipse is drawn, hold here and have students predict the extra condition. Ask them: "We added ninety-degree corners to turn a parallelogram into a rectangle; what single condition must we add to a rectangle to make it a square?" (attempt-before-reveal, expected answer: make all sides equal). Pause again around 2:05, just after Step 2 places point C, and ask "Why must the two new lines be parallel to AB and AD rather than any lines?" so students connect the construction back to the definition. After the video, have them guess the remaining two angles and the remaining two side lengths of the 4 cm by 5 cm parallelogram in their notebooks before moving to the next topic.

media.title: Playing with Quadrilaterals, Geoboard and Joining Triangles
media.context: Plays on M5.S6.T6.C60, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 165-second whiteboard-style animation on a pure white canvas. It opens on a geoboard dot grid where two rubber bands stretch perpendicular and equal-length as diagonals, drawn in Orange and Dark Green crossing at the centre, with their ends joined by a Navy Blue band to trace a square; a caption reads 'Step 1'. One diagonal then lengthens by 2 cm on both sides while the right-angle mark stays, the joined band redraws as a rhombus, and a side-tick label shows all four sides equal. The next panels slide cardboard triangle cutouts together edge to edge: two equilateral triangles of side 8 cm merge into a rhombus, two isosceles triangles (8, 8, 6) snap together along the 6 cm edge and again along an 8 cm edge to make two different shapes, and two scalene triangles (6, 9, 12) join along different shared edges, with on-screen captions naming each resulting quadrilateral as it forms.
media.teaching_notes: Play this video as a hands-on review after students have proved that perpendicular equal-length diagonals which bisect each other force a square, and before they try the joining-triangles task with their own cardboard cutouts. Pause around 0:45, right after the narrator asks what quadrilateral the equal perpendicular bisecting diagonals force, and have the class predict before the square is revealed, this is the attempt-before-reveal moment, so ask "which quadrilateral, and which three conditions are at work?" Pause again around 1:05, just as one diagonal is being extended, and ask "why did we do that, which single condition just broke, and what shape does that leave us with?" Tie the answer back to the difference between the square and the rhombus.
